title: Computer Power and Human Reason
subtitle: From Judgment to Calculation
pitch: The creator of the ELIZA chatbot was shocked that people confided in it. Here he argues there are tasks computers should never be given, whether or not they can do them.

chapters.g: Weizenbaum's simple program imitated a therapist, and people formed real emotional bonds with it, which alarmed him.
A careful explanation for general readers of what computers and programs really are.
Why programmers and society get drawn into treating computing as the model for everything.
Deciding is computing; choosing involves human values and wisdom that should not be handed over.
Some uses of computers are wrong even if possible, such as replacing human care with machines.
Researchers must ask whether their work should be done, not only whether it can be.

ideas: People project understanding onto even simple chatbots.
Some tasks should never be given to computers.

args.a: Computers should not replace human judgment in areas like care, justice and therapy.
args.c: Others argue that if machines do these tasks better and more fairly, refusing them has its own costs.

args.a: Treating everything as computation shrinks our idea of being human.
args.c: Computational views of the mind have been very productive in science, defenders say.

questions: Have you ever felt understood by a chatbot?
What task would you never give to an AI, even a perfect one?
Is the ELIZA effect stronger with today's models?

quiz.w: ELIZA was an early chatbot, built in the 1960s.
Even his secretary asked for privacy with it.
From judgment to calculation is the subtitle.
